source.title: Scaling Laws for Galaxy Images
source.authors: Mike Walmsley; Micah Bowles; Anna M. M. Scaife; Jason Shingirai Makechemu; Alexander J. Gordon; Annette M. N. Ferguson; Robert G. Mann; James Pearson; Jürgen J. Popp; Jo Bovy; Josh Speagle; Hugh Dickinson; Lucy Fortson; Tobias Géron; Sandor Kruk; Chris J. Lintott; Kameswara Mantha; Devina Mohan; David O'Ryan; Inigo V. Slijepevic

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures supervised scaling on galaxy images, a non-ImageNet image domain, and reports downstream results after in-domain pretraining.
record.gate_note: The study tests supervised image-data scaling and downstream effects of scaling in-domain pretraining. It does not test language-model parameter/token/compute laws or compute-optimal allocation. Figure 5 reports task-specific curves, but most task-by-task values are available only as plots; rows below use the paper’s stated aggregate results and its tabulated scaling fits.
record.test_reason: It fits supervised data-scaling laws for galaxy-image classifiers across five architecture families, and reports downstream effects of upstream scale. That is a new modality and setting for V5, with results bearing on V6 and V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also state that further supervised parameter scaling is unlikely to pay off given label limits, and that in-domain pretraining cuts downstream error by 31% on average. The scaling law itself is a linear fit of log-likelihood loss vs log data over a 4x range.
record.recipe_differences: Supervised multi-task galaxy-image training with a Dirichlet-Multinomial loss, rather than language-model next-token training; image test loss rather than held-out cross-entropy of language models; no token or compute-optimal allocation sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: Architecture family changes fitted intercepts and has somewhat different fitted gradients. Parameter-scaling gains depend on training-set size and task. Training recipes differ for MaxViT/ConvNeXT versus other families. The paper says downstream conclusions are robust to tested protocol hyperparameters.
record.problems: Upstream data scaling is reported over only a factor of four, and the authors state that testing beyond this range is not possible with available human labels. Parameter-scaling effects vary by task and dataset size. Downstream scaling comparisons are presented in plots without stated numerical values, and other smaller downstream datasets are omitted because split variance exceeds the scaling benefit. No compute-optimal allocation experiment is performed.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 5 shows task-specific data- and parameter-scaling curves and Figure 6 shows telescope-specific results, but the text does not provide separate numerical values for those plotted curves; the aggregate all-task result is recorded in R6. Figures 7 and 8 concern training/validation dynamics and overfitting rather than a direct power-law fit, so their plotted points are not separately transcribed. Other downstream performance comparisons in Figures 2 and 9 are not parameter- or upstream-scale sweeps.

untested.parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss; compute and token scaling.
No extrapolation from small runs to much larger runs.
No depth/width comparison at fixed parameter count.
Untested: video, repeated data, self-supervised training, compute scaling, and data ranges beyond 4x.
Downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss; a fitted downstream scaling law.

missing.what: Text statement that parameter scaling at 492k improves only some upstream tasks, with some plateauing near 20M parameters and others ('bar') showing no gain. This is declared in rows_left_out as plot-only, but the text states it explicitly and it should be a row.
missing.locator: Section 3 paragraph on Fig. 5; Fig. 5 caption

missing.what: Larger ConvNeXT models improve train loss far faster than test loss and overfit more at small data (4M-197M parameters).

record.verdict_notes: The 'power law' is a linear fit of loss vs log(images) on a linear-log plot, where the loss is a log-likelihood. Values are not directly comparable to LM loss exponents. The data range spans only a factor of four. MaxViT and ConvNeXT used a different training recipe.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss scaling in parameters, tokens, or compute.
The study does not fit on smaller runs and evaluate predictions against runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token split is tested.
Architecture families are compared, but the study does not isolate depth, width, or architecture effects at fixed parameter count to test whether they change loss only slightly.
Tests supervised galaxy-image data scaling, not image/video scaling generally, repeated-data training, or power laws for fine-tuning and transfer.
Reports downstream results for five galaxy tasks and upstream-scaling comparisons for two of them; does not test a general relationship between downstream performance and pretraining loss.

Reports architecture-family fit gradients and a stated deviation below the examined data range. Does not test parameter-count conventions, compute-optimal allocation, or whether published language-model laws disagree.

rows.subject: ResNet
rows.size_stated: ResNet variants; exact sizes not stated for this fit
rows.operation_detail: Fit a linear scaling relationship between labelled-image dataset size and upstream test loss.

conditions.value: study reports upstream data scaling across a factor of four; 120k to 490k images

rows.measure: Fitted gradient for test loss versus labelled data; the paper presents this as the power-law improvement rate.
rows.note: The authors say all architecture families show a similar rate of improvement; this fit is for the ResNet family.
rows.check: The fit is linear on a linear-log scale: Dirichlet-Multinomial loss vs log dataset size (footnote 3, App. A). The gradient is not a loss power-law exponent in the LM sense. Architecture-family similarity is not a V7 fit-choice test, so V7 is dropped.

source_check.correct: ResNet gradient -0.95, posterior 5th–95th percentiles (-1.07, -0.84). This is a gradient of loss versus log dataset size; V5 state: cannot_determine.
source_check.problem: The fitted linear-log gradient does not establish the power-law loss form specified by V5.

rows.subject: All tested architecture families and variants (aggregate)

conditions.value: 123k to 492k training images in the displayed comparisons

rows.measure: Upstream test loss as labelled-image count increases
rows.value: The paper reports a power-law improvement across all tested architectures and tasks; adding labelled images improved performance on every task.
rows.uncertainty: The paper reports min/max observed test-loss error bars; values not stated for this aggregate result.
rows.note: Aggregate statement by the authors; no single loss value is stated for all models or tasks.
rows.check: The range is only about 4x (123k-492k), not several orders of magnitude.

source_check.correct: The authors report consistent data-scaling improvements across architectures and tasks over approximately 123k–492k training images. The fitted relationship is linear in loss versus log dataset size; V5 state: cannot_determine.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3; Figures 4a and 5; footnote 3; Appendix A; Section 6.
source_check.problem: The attribution to the authors is accurate, but their terminology does not establish the same power-law loss form as V5.

rows.subject: Tested model families (aggregate; ResNet exception reported separately)
rows.size_stated: Model sizes range from small variants to approximately 100M parameters in the emphasized results
rows.operation_detail: Increase parameter count while training on 123k galaxy images and compare upstream test loss.

conditions.value: families other than the separately noted ResNet exception

rows.measure: Change in upstream test loss as parameter count increases
rows.baseline: smaller parameter counts at the same dataset size
rows.value: The paper reports little-to-no gains from parameter scaling.
rows.note: This is the authors’ aggregate characterization; ResNet is identified as an exception.
rows.check: At 123k images, data is the bottleneck. Absent parameter gains are therefore consistent with the bottleneck clause of the scaling claim, not evidence against it.

source_check.correct: At 123k images, parameter scaling provides little-to-no improvement except for ResNet. The parameter-scaling power-law form is not established; V5 state: cannot_determine.
source_check.problem: Negligible gains under data limitation do not establish absence of the power-law effect specified by V5.
